subChunks.title: Place, Community & the Psychology of the Built Environment
subChunks.hookHtml: In the 1970s, researchers at the University of Michigan began studying how urban environments affected human psychology. Roger Ulrich's (1984) landmark study, published in Science, found that surgical patients whose hospital room window faced a view of trees had significantly shorter postoperative hospital stays, required fewer analgesics, and received more positive evaluations from nurses than patients whose windows faced a brick wall. The only difference between the groups was what they could see. This finding — later replicated many times across different contexts — suggested something that seems intuitive but had rarely been studied rigorously: the physical environment shapes psychological states, health outcomes, and behaviour in measurable, consequential ways. Environmental psychology is the systematic study of person-environment relationships — how physical settings (urban density, green space, noise, light, temperature, architectural design) influence psychological wellbeing, cognition, social behaviour, and health. Community psychology extends this to the social environment — asking how neighbourhood characteristics, social capital, collective efficacy, and community institutions shape individual and collective wellbeing. Together, these perspectives offer something that purely individual-focused psychology cannot: an account of how the contexts in which people live their lives shape what is possible for them — and what psychologists can do by intervening at the environmental and community level rather than (only) at the individual level.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Attention Restoration Theory (Kaplan & Kaplan)

Kaplan and Kaplan's (1989) Attention Restoration Theory (ART) proposes that directed attention — the effortful, voluntary attention required for most cognitive tasks — is a limited resource that becomes fatigued with sustained use. Natural environments restore this resource through: (1) fascination — involuntary, effortless attention to natural stimuli (water, plants, sky); (2) being away — psychological distance from demands of everyday life; (3) extent — richness and coherence of the environment; and (4) compatibility — fit between environment and individual needs and inclinations.

Research consistently shows that exposure to natural environments — parks, trees, water — reduces directed attention fatigue, improves cognitive performance, reduces physiological stress markers, and enhances mood. This has informed urban planning (street tree planting, park provision), hospital design (window views), school design (schoolyard greenery), and workplace design (natural light, plant life). The effects are robust even for brief exposures: a 20-minute walk in a park produces measurable improvements in attention and mood relative to urban walking.

Stress and the Urban Environment

Urban environments are associated with higher rates of depression, anxiety, and psychosis than rural environments — though the relationship is complex and partially explained by selective migration (people with mental health difficulties may move to cities, not only develop problems in cities). Several environmental stressors are implicated:

  • Noise pollution: Chronic noise exposure (road traffic, aircraft) is associated with elevated cortisol, sleep disturbance, cardiovascular risk, and impaired cognitive development in children. The WHO identifies noise as the second most harmful environmental stressor in Western Europe after air pollution.
  • Population density and crowding: High density is associated with stress, reduced prosocial behaviour, and social withdrawal — the 'social withdrawal' response to urban density was documented in Milgram's (1970) work on urban overload. However, density effects interact with sense of control and choice — choosing density (urban living preferences) moderates its negative effects.
  • Air pollution: PM2.5 particulate matter exposure is associated with depression, anxiety, and cognitive decline, over and above other risk factors.
  • Green space access: Proximity to green space buffers stress and is associated with better mental health, physical activity, and neighbourhood social cohesion — independently of socioeconomic factors.

Community Psychology: Theory and Practice

Community psychology (Rappaport, 1977; Dalton et al.) emerged in the 1960s as a response to the limitations of individual clinical practice for addressing population-level mental health problems. Its core principles:

  • Ecological perspective: Individuals exist within nested ecological contexts — settings, communities, macrosystems — and problems cannot be understood or addressed at the individual level alone
  • Prevention over treatment: Primary prevention (preventing problems before they develop) and secondary prevention (early intervention) are prioritised over tertiary treatment of established disorder
  • Empowerment: Community psychology is committed to increasing communities' capacity to identify and solve their own problems rather than imposing expert solutions from outside
  • Social justice: Structural inequalities — poverty, racism, discrimination — are understood as root causes of individual psychological distress; community psychologists engage with advocacy and social change
  • Diversity and inclusion: Community psychology practice must be responsive to cultural, economic, and social diversity

Sense of community (McMillan & Chavis, 1986): A psychological sense of belonging, mutual influence, and shared emotional connection within a community setting. Sense of community predicts wellbeing, civic participation, and collective efficacy — communities with higher sense of community show greater capacity for collective action to address shared problems.

Social capital (Putnam): The networks of relationships and norms of reciprocity within communities. Bonding social capital (strong ties within homogeneous groups) provides support and solidarity; bridging social capital (weak ties across diverse groups) provides information, opportunity, and social cohesion. Communities with high social capital are more resilient to adversity and show better health outcomes at the population level.

Collective Efficacy and Neighbourhood Crime

Sampson, Raudenbush, and Earls' (1997) landmark Chicago study found that neighbourhood collective efficacy — the combination of social cohesion and willingness to intervene for the common good — was the strongest neighbourhood-level predictor of violent crime rates, independent of socioeconomic disadvantage and other standard predictors. Neighbourhoods with high collective efficacy could maintain informal social control even under conditions of poverty — a finding that challenged purely economic explanations of urban crime and pointed toward the importance of community social processes for population wellbeing.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen shows two images side by side: a hospital room with a window looking onto a car park, and one looking onto trees and a garden. 'Which of these patients recovers faster?' she asks. Nobody is surprised. 'Then why,' she continues, 'are most NHS hospital rooms designed like the first?'

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Environmental psychology produces findings that feel obvious once you know them but have enormous policy implications that are systematically ignored. Green space access is associated with better mental health. Chronic noise is associated with cardiovascular risk and impaired child development. Urban design that increases social interaction is associated with lower crime. These are not soft findings — they are replicable effects with consequences that would be enormous at population level. The gap between what the evidence shows and what gets built is itself a social science problem worth studying.

storyBeats.speaker: Collective efficacy and crime
storyBeats.text: Sampson et al.'s (1997) Chicago Neighbourhood Study measured collective efficacy in 343 neighbourhoods through survey items asking residents whether neighbours could be counted on to intervene if, for example, children were skipping school, graffiti appeared, or a fight broke out. Collective efficacy — not poverty, racial composition, or population density — was the most powerful neighbourhood predictor of violent crime rates, explaining 70% of the variance in violence between neighbourhoods. The finding challenged the assumption that urban crime is simply a product of disadvantage, suggesting that social processes within communities — trust, social norms, willingness to act — are critical protective factors that can be maintained even in poor communities and that policy should actively support.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Community psychology makes a claim that is important and uncomfortable for individual-focused clinicians: if the problem is structural, the solution has to be structural too. You cannot therapy your way out of systemic poverty or environmental disadvantage. The individual clinical encounter matters — deeply — but it is one tool among many, and not always the most powerful one. Community psychology asks what would happen if we invested the same resources we spend on individual treatment in prevention, community building, and structural change. The answer is almost certainly: a lot.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A local authority is commissioning a new housing estate for 800 families on the site of a former industrial area in a post-industrial city. The authority has a limited budget and must prioritise design decisions. A consultant psychologist has been asked to advise on which design features would most improve the mental health and wellbeing of the future residents.

  1. Using Attention Restoration Theory and the evidence on green space, advise on one specific design feature that should be prioritised, with evidence for its expected effects.
  2. Using the collective efficacy and social capital research, advise on two design features that could support community cohesion and collective action among residents.
  3. A council member argues that 'psychological research on environment is irrelevant because individual mental health is primarily genetic and clinical — not a product of where you live.' Critically evaluate this argument using evidence from environmental and community psychology.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Green space design recommendation: Incorporate accessible green spaces — parks, tree-lined streets, communal gardens — within walking distance (ideally within 300m) of all dwellings. Evidence base: Ulrich's foundational study and subsequent systematic reviews consistently show that green space access is associated with reduced depression, anxiety, and perceived stress, reduced cortisol and physiological stress markers, improved cognitive restoration (Kaplan & Kaplan's ART), increased physical activity, and improved social cohesion (shared green spaces promote incidental social interaction). A 2019 WHO Europe review found that people living in greener neighbourhoods have measurably lower rates of depression and mental health service use, independent of socioeconomic factors. The effect is dose-responsive — more greenery, within range, produces greater benefits. Given budget constraints, tree planting in streets (low cost, high environmental benefit) and a central communal green space (gathering and activity point) are high-impact, cost-effective investments. Design specifics matter: green spaces should be safe, well-maintained, and designed for multiple uses (children's play, adult socialising, quiet rest) to maximise accessibility across the population.

2. Two community cohesion design features: (a) Mixed-use communal spaces: Provide communal spaces that serve multiple functions — a community centre or hall that can host group activities, meetings, and informal gatherings. Research on collective efficacy (Sampson et al., 1997) shows that social trust and willingness to act for the common good are key protective factors for community wellbeing; communal spaces where residents can meet and interact create the conditions for trust and social norms to develop. Design feature: a central community hall with flexible space, located centrally and easily accessible, with a programme of community activities in the first two years supported by community development workers. (b) Human-scale streetscape and mixed amenities: Design streets to be walkable, with ground-floor retail and services that encourage 'eyes on the street' (natural surveillance), reduce car dominance, and create destinations that residents visit regularly. Jane Jacobs' urban design principles — short blocks, mixed uses, buildings of varied age — increase spontaneous social interaction and the sense of community. Research supports walkable neighbourhoods with local amenities for social capital formation and sense of community; communities where residents regularly encounter each other in informal settings develop higher social trust.

3. Evaluation of the council member's argument: The claim that mental health is 'primarily genetic and clinical — not a product of where you live' is empirically incorrect at the population level. Behavioural genetics research does confirm substantial heritability for many mental health conditions — but heritability is a population-level statistic that says nothing about what proportion of mental health variability is caused by environment in a given population. Gene-environment interaction research consistently shows that environmental context substantially moderates genetic risk — the same genetic vulnerability produces very different outcomes in supportive vs. adverse environments. The evidence from environmental psychology and community psychology is direct and compelling: (a) Green space access independently predicts depression and anxiety rates across large population studies, controlling for socioeconomic factors; (b) Neighbourhood collective efficacy predicts violent crime rates and safety perceptions, with downstream mental health consequences; (c) Urban-rural differences in psychosis rates are robust even after controlling for selection effects — urban environments contribute independently to psychosis risk; (d) The Marmot social gradient shows that health and mental health improve at every step up the socioeconomic and environmental hierarchy — a gradient that genetics alone cannot explain. Genes and clinical factors matter enormously. So does environment. Framing these as alternatives rather than interacting determinants misrepresents the science.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml: Community psychologists argue that the dominant model of psychological practice — individual therapy delivered by trained professionals to people who seek help — is an inherently limited response to population-level mental health challenges. Critically evaluate this argument and assess what a more comprehensive population-level approach to mental health might look like. Aim for 250–300 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The community psychology critique of individualised therapy has substantial force. Epidemiological data consistently show that only a minority of people with mental health difficulties ever receive treatment — the 'treatment gap' is estimated at 75–90% in low-income countries and 30–60% in high-income countries. Individual therapy, requiring trained professionals, extended treatment time, and individual help-seeking, is a resource-intensive approach that systematically fails to reach many of the people who need it most. Furthermore, much mental health distress has social-structural causes — poverty, housing insecurity, discrimination, adverse childhood experiences — that individual therapy addresses only in the sense of helping people cope with conditions that should be changed.

However, the critique risks understating what individual therapy can offer. For people with established clinical-level disorders — PTSD, severe depression, psychosis — evidence-based individual and group therapies produce genuine recovery that prevention alone does not achieve. The choice is not 'individual therapy or structural change' — both are necessary, and they address different problems at different stages.

A more comprehensive population-level approach would include: (1) Primary prevention — addressing social determinants (housing, employment, income security, green space access, community cohesion) that are upstream causes of population-level mental health; (2) Universal programmes — school mental health curricula, parenting programmes, workplace mental health standards that build resilience and reduce incidence; (3) Stepped care systems — providing effective self-help, digital, and group-based interventions at scale before intensive individual therapy; (4) Community development — building collective efficacy and social capital in communities with high need; (5) Individual therapy — available as a higher-intensity option for established disorders.

The real failure is not individual therapy itself — it is health systems that invest heavily in treatment and insufficiently in prevention and structural improvement.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old why being able to see trees or a park from your home might actually affect your mental health — what psychological mechanism might explain the effect, and why this matters for how we design cities.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Kaplan and Kaplan's (1989) theory that natural environments restore directed attention through fascination (involuntary, effortless attention to natural stimuli), being away (psychological distance from demands), extent (richness of the environment), and compatibility with individual needs. Underpins research on green space and cognitive restoration.

Sampson et al.'s (1997) concept combining social cohesion and willingness to intervene for the common good within a neighbourhood. The strongest neighbourhood-level predictor of violent crime rates in the Chicago study, independent of socioeconomic disadvantage.

Putnam's concept of the networks of relationships and norms of reciprocity within communities. Distinguishes bonding social capital (strong ties within homogeneous groups) from bridging social capital (weak ties across diverse groups). High social capital is associated with better population health outcomes.

In community psychology and public health, interventions targeting an entire population before disorder develops — aimed at reducing incidence by addressing risk factors and strengthening protective factors. Contrasted with secondary prevention (early intervention) and tertiary treatment.

questions.questionHtml: What are the four components of natural environments proposed by Kaplan and Kaplan's Attention Restoration Theory to explain their restorative effects?
options: Fresh air, natural light, silence, and physical exercise
Fascination, being away, extent, and compatibility
Safety, beauty, biodiversity, and sensory richness
Novelty, predictability, social interaction, and physical comfort
questions.correctAnswer: Fascination, being away, extent, and compatibility
questions.explanationHtml: Kaplan and Kaplan's (1989) Attention Restoration Theory proposes that natural environments restore depleted directed attention through four properties: (1) Fascination — natural environments capture involuntary, effortless attention (water, trees, birds, clouds), giving directed attention a rest without requiring effort; (2) Being away — natural environments provide psychological distance from the demands, schedules, and cognitive load of everyday life; (3) Extent — natural environments are rich, coherent, and expansive enough to constitute a whole other world to explore, sustaining engagement; (4) Compatibility — natural environments fit with many people's inclinations and needs, requiring little resistance or effort to engage with. Together these components explain why time in natural settings reliably reduces attentional fatigue and improves subsequent cognitive performance in empirical studies.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: Research by Sampson and colleagues found that neighbourhood poverty level was the strongest predictor of violent crime rates across Chicago neighbourhoods.
questions.explanationHtml: False. Sampson, Raudenbush, and Earls' (1997) landmark Chicago study found that neighbourhood collective efficacy — the combination of social cohesion and willingness to intervene for the common good — was the strongest neighbourhood-level predictor of violent crime rates, explaining 70% of the variance in violence between neighbourhoods. This was independent of, and statistically more powerful than, poverty, racial composition, and population density. The finding challenged purely economic explanations of urban crime and demonstrated that social processes within communities — trust, shared norms, willingness to act — are critical protective factors that can be maintained even in economically disadvantaged communities. It has important policy implications: investments in community cohesion and collective efficacy may be as important as poverty reduction for reducing violence rates.

questions.questionHtml: A mental health charity proposes expanding individual CBT provision to increase access for people currently on waiting lists. A community psychologist argues instead for investment in a neighbourhood green space project and a community development worker programme. How should these two proposals be evaluated?
options: The CBT expansion is always preferable — individual therapy has stronger evidence than environmental interventions

The proposals address different levels of intervention and both have evidence; the best strategy depends on the specific population, the presenting problems, and whether the goal is treatment of established disorder or prevention of future incidence
The community approach is always preferable because individual therapy medicalises social problems
The proposals are mutually exclusive and organisations must choose one
questions.correctAnswer: The proposals address different levels of intervention and both have evidence; the best strategy depends on the specific population, the presenting problems, and whether the goal is treatment of established disorder or prevention of future incidence
questions.explanationHtml: Both proposals have evidence and address real needs at different levels. CBT expansion addresses the treatment gap for people with established mental health disorders who are currently not receiving evidence-based care — a genuine and significant problem. Green space and community development address upstream social and environmental determinants of mental health, potentially preventing future incidence across a large population, but will not reach people with established clinical-level disorders who need individual treatment. The most effective population-level mental health strategy uses both in a stepped care framework: environmental and community-level prevention reduces incidence; accessible digital and group-based self-help manages mild-moderate distress; individual evidence-based therapy treats established disorders. The appropriate balance depends on the specific needs of the population, the available resources, and whether short-term treatment or longer-term prevention is the priority. Neither proposal is inherently superior to the other — they address different problems at different timescales.
